item.title: Ebola Fatality Rate Tops 50% After Hundreds of Deaths Added to Congo Toll
item.description: The death rate among confirmed Ebola cases in the Democratic Republic of Congo has climbed above 50% after health authorities added hundreds of previously unallocated fatalities to the official toll.
item.dc:creator: list.metadata.agency
item.content:encoded: (Bloomberg) -- The death rate among confirmed Ebola cases in the Democratic Republic of Congo has climbed above 50% after health authorities added hundreds of previously unallocated fatalities to the official toll.The outbreak has caused 10,414 confirmed infections and 5,372 deaths, giving it a reported case-fatality ratio of 51.6%, the National Institute of Public Health said in its most recent report released Saturday.A review of records across 97% of affected health zones in Ituri, the epidemic’s epicenter, resulted in 314 earlier Ebola deaths being added to the province’s cumulative toll, health officials said.The adjustment pushed the reported fatality ratio up from 48.6% two days earlier, even as the number of confirmed infections rose by just 140.The revision comes as health authorities continue to report dozens of new infections a day from an epidemic that has spread to eight provinces and 67 health zones. It is the largest Ebola outbreak in Congo’s history and the largest globally after the 2013-2016 epidemic in West Africa.The outbreak has also spilled beyond the country, though transmission elsewhere remains limited. Nigeria said Saturday that two suspected cases in Adamawa state tested negative after two rounds of testing, leaving the country with one confirmed infection.The US said on Sunday it will further tighten travel restrictions in response to the outbreak: Beginning late Tuesday, anyone boarding an international flight to the US must attest that they haven’t been in the Democratic Republic of Congo during the previous 21 days, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Travelers who have been in the country during that period generally won’t be allowed to board US-bound commercial flights.More stories like this are available on bloomberg.com©2026 Bloomberg L.P.

item.title: UK Tries to Map Out Risks to Public Services of Extreme Weather
item.description: Extreme weather is having a measurable impact on Britain’s public finances as areas including railways, prisons and healthcare are increasingly affected, the UK’s National Audit Office said.
item.dc:creator: list.metadata.agency
item.content:encoded: (Bloomberg) -- Extreme weather is having a measurable impact on Britain’s public finances as areas including railways, prisons and healthcare are increasingly affected, the UK’s National Audit Office said. The full scale of the damage remains difficult to gauge, however, as many government departments are failing to provide the disclosures needed for a proper assessment, the NAO said in a report published on Monday.“Parliament needs clear information on the resilience of infrastructure, service provision and finances to climate change, and on how these risks are being managed,” said Gareth Davies, head of the NAO, in a statement. “We expect this reporting to become more useful over time.”This is the first year in which larger UK government departments have been required to publish the full details of the risks they face due to global warming. In many cases, efforts to understand such exposures remain at an early stage, the NAO said. Disclosures are necessary to help lawmakers keep track of how prepared the UK’s public services are, it said. Britons are facing increasingly severe — and in some cases deadly — periods of extreme heat followed by flash floods. Intense heat has already resulted in damage to roads and railways, and left schools and hospitals dangerously hot this summer. At the same time, floods are becoming more frequent and more destructive to key infrastructure such as railways. Flooding was the most common hazard identified in the disclosures monitored by the NAO. Some 89% of prisons face a high risk of flooding, while sites managed by the National Health Service saw 391 flooding incidents in 2024-25. Among the many impacts of overheating is the tendency toward more violence in prisons, the NAO report found. “Government still has much to do, particularly in setting meaningful targets,” said Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, chair of the UK Parliament’s Committee of Public Accounts, commenting on the NAO’s findings. “Better reporting is encouraging, but Parliament and the public need more than a list of risks: they need to know how prepared government is to manage them.”More stories like this are available on bloomberg.com©2026 Bloomberg L.P.

item.title: Why Wendy’s is struggling in US burger market and has become a potential takeover target for Nelson Peltz | Explained
item.description: Wendy’s is losing customers to rivals as sales fall, costs rise and its recovery plans face pressure. Nelson Peltz’s Trian Fund has now made a $1.4 billion offer to take the burger chain private, putting its future under fresh scrutiny.
item.dc:creator: Trisha Bhattacharya
item.content:encoded: Wendy’s, once one of the biggest names in the American burger business, is facing a difficult period as customers move towards competitors and its sales continue to fall. The fast-food chain, known for its square burgers and Frosty desserts, has struggled to keep pace with rivals such as McDonald’s and Burger King.Its problems have now attracted the attention of billionaire investor Nelson Peltz. His investment firm, Trian Fund Management, along with a group of partners, has made an offer worth around $1.4 billion to take Wendy’s private. The proposal values the company at $7.35 per share in cash.Why is Wendy's losing the burger wars and why is Nelson Peltz eyeing the company?Wendy’s confirmed on October 28 that it had received the unsolicited, non-binding offer. This means the proposal is not a completed takeover agreement. The company’s board has formed an independent committee to examine it, and there is no guarantee that the deal will go ahead. The offer comes at a time when Wendy’s is dealing with falling sales, weaker customer traffic, rising food costs and pressure on its franchise business. The company has also struggled to find a clear direction after several changes in its top leadership. Wendy’s was founded in 1969 by Dave Thomas, who named the restaurant after his daughter. It became popular for its square beef patties, chilli and Frosty desserts. Its advertising campaigns, particularly the famous “Where’s the beef?” slogan, also helped it stand out in the American fast-food market. For years, Wendy’s was the second-largest burger chain in the US, behind McDonald’s. However, it has since slipped behind Burger King, which has been working to improve its restaurants and menu. According to data cited by Fortune, Wendy’s share of US burger-chain sales fell from 11.5% in 2019 to 10.4% in 2025. The company has also struggled to bring customers back to its restaurants. In its most recent reported quarter, sales at established US restaurants fell 7%, marking the sixth consecutive quarterly decline. Visits to its US outlets dropped 12.5%. The chain is also facing pressure from rising costs. Beef prices have affected its profits, while inflation has made many customers more careful about spending on restaurant meals. Lower-income consumers, an important customer group for fast-food companies, have cut back as prices have increased. Wendy’s has also faced criticism over its value offerings and the quality of its restaurant experience. Its recent promotions and new menu items have not delivered the response the company hoped for. The breakfast business, another area where it has tried to grow, has also failed to become a major success. Wendy’s CEO Bob Wright has acknowledged the problems. “Our quality differentiation has eroded, our value proposition has weakened, and we have not consistently delivered the experience customers expect from Wendy’s,” he said. What is Nelson Peltz offering, and why does he want to take Wendy’s private? Trian Fund Management already has a significant holding in Wendy’s, with a stake of around 16.3%. The latest proposal has been made alongside Flynn Group, BlueFive Capital and Sixth Street Partners. The group has offered $7.35 in cash for each share of Wendy’s that it does not already own. The offer values the transaction at approximately $1.4 billion. It represents a premium of nearly 19% over Wendy’s closing share price on October 27, according to Reuters. Peltz believes the company needs a longer period to rebuild its business. Taking Wendy’s private could allow its owners to focus on improving operations without the pressure of public-market investors and quarterly financial results. In a letter to Wendy’s board, Peltz wrote, “Wendy’s sits at a critical juncture”. He also argued that the company needed significant investment to reduce its debt and carry out the changes required to improve its performance.The proposal is not Peltz's first attempt to explore a private ownership arrangement. Trian considered a similar move in 2022 but later decided against it. The investment firm has held shares in Wendy’s since 2005.

item.title: OPEC+ keeps December oil output unchanged: Why Iran war disruptions cloud 2027 production plans
item.description: OPEC+ has kept December oil production targets unchanged as the Iran war continues to disrupt Gulf exports. With most members pumping below targets, the alliance faces uncertainty over 2027 quotas, amid concerns about supply recovery through the Strait of Hormuz and a possible global oil surplus.
item.dc:creator: Livemint
item.content:encoded: OPEC+ oil-producing countries have kept their December production targets unchanged, signalling that the group is unlikely to make further changes to its output policy until next year as the Iran war continues to disrupt oil exports from the Middle East, Reuters reported. The decision was taken at an online meeting on Sunday by seven key members — Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Algeria, Kazakhstan and Oman. The group said in a statement that it would maintain its existing production targets for December. The move comes as Gulf producers attempt to increase exports despite months of disruption caused by the conflict. However, most are still producing well below their agreed targets, limiting the amount of additional oil reaching global markets. OPEC+ holds output steady ahead of key November meeting The seven countries have been responsible for monthly production decisions in recent years. The wider OPEC+ alliance includes the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) and other producers, including Russia. The United Arab Emirates was also part of the group involved in monthly output decisions until it left OPEC in May. All 21 members of the wider OPEC+ alliance are scheduled to meet on November 29. Analysts cited by Reuters expect the meeting to be more significant, as the group is likely to discuss production quotas for 2027. "Today's decision was the easy one," Jorge Leon, an analyst at Rystad, told Reuters. He said the more important test would come at the November 29 ministerial meeting, when members decide the framework for production in 2027. Iran war and Strait of Hormuz add to oil market uncertainty The decision comes amid continued uncertainty over oil supplies from the Middle East. The Iran war has disrupted exports from the Gulf, while the possibility of further escalation has added to concerns about global supply. However, the longer-term outlook remains uncertain. The International Energy Agency and other forecasters have warned that the market could face excess supply in 2027 if oil flows from the Gulf return to normal. Leon said OPEC+ faced a difficult decision on its 2027 production plans, given uncertainty over the US-Iran conflict, the recovery of shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and the potential surplus once disrupted supplies return to the market. OPEC+ reviews production capacity before setting 2027 quotas The seven countries have increased their output targets through much of 2026. In September, they completed the phased rollback of a production cut of 1.65 million barrels per day (bpd), which had been agreed in 2023. Before Sunday's decision, the group had also kept its production targets unchanged for October and November. However, another layer of production cuts, amounting to around 2 million bpd and covering most OPEC+ members, remains in place until the end of 2026. The alliance is also reviewing the production capacity of its members before deciding the 2027 output baselines. These baselines will determine future quotas and influence how the group plans to unwind the remaining supply cuts. The review is expected to be completed by mid-November, according to Reuters. The Iran war has disrupted projects aimed at expanding oil production capacity across the Middle East, making it harder to estimate how much individual countries will be able to produce in the coming years. The findings will be important for OPEC+ as it prepares its 2027 production framework amid uncertainty over regional exports, future supply and global oil demand. With inputs from Reuters.

item.title: Why Elon Musk is weighing a Tesla-SpaceX merger: What a combined entity could mean for his business empire and investors
item.description: Elon Musk is weighing a potential merger between Tesla and SpaceX, a move that could create a $3.5 trillion technology giant. With both companies expanding into AI, robotics, semiconductors, a merger could unlock synergies but also raise regulatory, and governance concerns for investors.
item.dc:creator: Bhanu Pratap
item.content:encoded: Elon Musk is considering bringing two of his biggest business ventures, electric vehicle maker Tesla and rocket manufacturer SpaceX, under one corporate umbrella in a move that could create one of the world's most valuable companies and reshape his sprawling technology empire.The world's richest person publicly backed the idea when asked whether merging the two companies would make sense, responding with an unequivocal "Yes".The proposal appears to be gaining traction, with Musk revealing that special committees have been formed to examine a potential deal.However, he cautioned that there is no certainty that a merger will take place and that no agreement has been reached.With Tesla valued at approximately $1.5 trillion and SpaceX at around $2 trillion, a combination could create an entity worth nearly $3.5 trillion.Such a transaction would rank among the largest corporate mergers in history, although it would require shareholder approval and face significant regulatory and corporate governance challenges.The prospect of a merger comes as Musk increasingly connects his businesses through investments in AI, robotics, semiconductor manufacturing, satellite communications and advanced computing infrastructure.Here's why Musk is considering the merger and what a combined company could mean for his business empire and investors.Why does Elon Musk want to combine Tesla and SpaceX?A merger could bring several interconnected parts of Musk's business ambitions under one corporate structure, creating a technology and manufacturing ecosystem spanning transportation, energy, robotics, communications and space exploration.Musk believes closer cooperation between the two companies could accelerate development in areas such as AI, advanced chip design, robotics and next-generation computing infrastructure."There's a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software, chip design, the Terafab obviously, robotics, mass-to-orbit with the Starmind constellation (of orbital data centers), connectivity," he said.The move could also have implications for Musk's influence over the combined entity. He has previously raised concerns about his level of control at Tesla as the company expands its AI and robotics ambitions.What would a Tesla-SpaceX merger mean for investors?For investors, a merger would offer exposure to a significantly broader range of businesses through a single corporate entity.Tesla shareholders would gain exposure to SpaceX's rocket-launch operations, its Starlink satellite internet business and future space-based ventures.Conversely, SpaceX investors would acquire an interest in Tesla's electric vehicles, battery storage systems, autonomous driving technology and humanoid robotics ambitions.A combined valuation of approximately $3.5 trillion would place the company among the world's largest corporations, with interests spanning automobiles, energy storage, satellite communications, space transportation and AI infrastructure.However, the arrangement would also expose investors to a wider range of business and financial risks. Tesla's automotive and energy operations function in markets very different from SpaceX's rocket launches and satellite services, according to Reuters. Where could Tesla and SpaceX collaborate?The two companies have several potential areas of technological overlap, particularly in AI, computing, energy and advanced manufacturing.One of the biggest opportunities lies in semiconductor production and computing infrastructure. Musk has outlined plans for Terafab, a semiconductor and AI-computing project intended to manufacture advanced chips for Tesla's autonomous vehicles and Optimus humanoid robots, as well as SpaceX's AI and data-centre ambitions. Musk hopes the project can begin volume production by late 2028.Energy is another area where the companies could benefit from closer coordination.Tesla's expertise in batteries and large-scale energy storage could help meet the growing electricity requirements of SpaceX's computing infrastructure, including proposed data-centre projects.Starlink's satellite network could also provide connectivity for Tesla's autonomous vehicles, robotaxis and future generations of Optimus robots, particularly in areas where conventional communication networks are limited, according to a Reuters report.Manufacturing presents another opportunity. Tesla's experience in large-scale factory automation could complement SpaceX's efforts to industrialise Starship production.What are the risks of a Tesla-SpaceX merger?Despite the potential technological and operational benefits, combining the two companies would bring considerable regulatory, geopolitical and execution challenges.One major concern is their differing exposure to international markets and national-security interests. SpaceX is a major contractor for the US military, intelligence agencies and NASA.Tesla, meanwhile, has substantial manufacturing and commercial operations in China, including its large Shanghai factory, which plays an important role in its global business.Bringing the companies under one corporate structure could attract greater scrutiny from US regulators and national-security authorities, according to Reuters.It could also complicate Tesla's relationship with Beijing, given the strategic importance of SpaceX's government contracts and satellite operations.Shareholder approval and corporate governance would present further hurdles. Investors would need to be convinced that the combination creates value for both businesses and that their respective valuations, assets and liabilities are fairly accounted for.There is also the challenge of execution. Starship, robotaxis, humanoid robots, AI data centres and orbital computing infrastructure are all capital-intensive projects involving significant technological uncertainties.Combining Tesla and SpaceX would not eliminate these risks.With inputs from Reuters.
